courses.title: Tier 2: Advanced Windows Troubleshooting
courses.description: Go beyond restarts — diagnose boot failures, blue screens, and broken profiles, and recover Windows with the tools Tier 2 is expected to wield.

content.intro: When Windows won't start, knowing the boot sequence tells you which stage failed and which tool fixes it.

sections.caption: Windows boot stages — identify where it fails to target the fix.

ul.t: no display, beeps — hardware or boot device order.
'no boot device' / BCD errors — repair with WinRE.
stuck logo or reboot loop — often a bad driver/update.
(in WinRE) fixes many boot/BCD issues automatically.
rebuilds boot configuration from the command prompt.

note.text: Three failed boots normally drops Windows into the Recovery Environment (WinRE) automatically.

content.practice: Describe which tool you'd reach for if a PC shows a 'Boot Device Not Found' message versus a spinning-logo reboot loop.

quiz.p: A 'no boot device / BCD' error is best fixed with…
quiz.ex: WinRE's Startup Repair or bootrec fixes boot/BCD problems.

quiz.p: Windows normally enters WinRE automatically after…
quiz.ex: Repeated (≈3) boot failures trigger WinRE.

quiz.p: A reboot loop after the logo most often points to…
quiz.ex: Kernel-stage loops are commonly driver/update related.

content.intro: A blue screen (BSOD) isn't random — the stop code and crash dump point at the cause.

p: The stop code (e.g. DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA) and any named driver file are your first clues — search the exact code.

ul.t: a timeline of crashes and what changed.
C:\Windows\Minidump — analysable for the faulting driver.
new hardware, driver, or update just before it started.

note.text: Faulty RAM, storage errors, and bad/mismatched drivers cause most BSODs — test memory and roll back recent drivers.

content.practice: For a PC that started blue-screening after a graphics driver update, outline your first two diagnostic steps.

quiz.p: The first clue to a BSOD's cause is…
o: The stop code (and any named driver)
quiz.ex: The stop code and faulting driver point to the cause.

quiz.p: Which tool shows a timeline of crashes and recent changes?
quiz.ex: Reliability Monitor correlates crashes with changes.

quiz.p: Frequent BSODs with memory-related stop codes suggest testing…
quiz.ex: Memory errors are a common BSOD cause — run a memory test.

content.intro: Safe Mode and WinRE let you fix a system that can't boot normally by loading a minimal environment.

p: Boots with only essential drivers/services — if the problem disappears, a third-party driver or startup item is the cause. Use it to uninstall a bad driver or run cleanup.

ul.b: Startup Repair, Command Prompt, System Restore
ul.t: — all launch from WinRE.
— enable Safe Mode and other boot options.

note.text: Hold Shift and click Restart, or interrupt boot three times, to reach the Advanced Startup / recovery options.

content.practice: A laptop boots fine in Safe Mode but crashes normally — state what that tells you and your next step.

quiz.p: If a problem disappears in Safe Mode, the cause is likely…
o: A third-party driver or startup item
quiz.ex: Safe Mode loads minimal drivers, isolating third-party causes.

quiz.p: Startup Repair and System Restore are launched from…
quiz.ex: WinRE hosts the recovery tools.

quiz.p: A quick way to reach Advanced Startup is…
quiz.ex: Shift+Restart opens Advanced Startup options.

content.intro: When configuration breaks, these tools roll Windows back — and the registry is where much of that configuration lives.

p: Reverts system files, drivers, and registry to an earlier restore point without touching personal files — ideal after a bad update or install.

ul.t: reinstalls Windows, keeps documents (removes apps).
a clean wipe for reassignment.

note.text: The registry stores system/app settings in hives (HKLM, HKCU). Back up a key before editing (File → Export) — a wrong change can break Windows.

content.practice: Choose the right tool for: a bad update broke the system, versus preparing a laptop for a new employee.

quiz.p: System Restore reverts…
o: System files, drivers, and registry to a restore point
quiz.ex: It rolls back system state without deleting personal files.

quiz.p: 'Reset this PC → Keep my files' will…
o: Reinstall Windows and keep documents (removes apps)
quiz.ex: It refreshes Windows, keeping files but removing apps.

quiz.p: Before editing a registry key you should…
quiz.ex: Export the key so you can restore it if needed.

content.intro: For repeated builds and unrecoverable machines, reimaging restores a known-good standard image fast.

p: A standard image gives every machine the same OS, apps, and settings — faster than rebuilding by hand and consistent to support.

ul: Back up user data (profiles, local files)
Note apps, printers, and mapped drives to restore
Confirm drivers for the model are available

note.text: Rejoin the domain, restore data, reinstall role-specific apps, and verify updates — then hand back.

content.practice: List the pre-reimage checklist you'd run so a user loses nothing when their machine is reimaged.

quiz.p: A standard image mainly provides…
quiz.ex: Imaging gives consistent, fast, supportable builds.

quiz.p: The critical step before reimaging is to…
quiz.ex: Always back up user data before a wipe.

quiz.p: After reimaging a domain PC you must…
o: Rejoin the domain and restore data/apps
quiz.ex: Rejoin the domain and restore the user's environment.

courses.title: Tier 2: Active Directory for Support
courses.description: Handle the AD tasks that land on Tier 2 — managing accounts and OUs, fixing access via groups, resolving lockouts, and knowing what Group Policy is doing.

content.intro: Most Tier 2 AD work is account lifecycle: creating, moving, disabling, and organising users in the right place.

ul: Create with correct attributes (name, UPN, department)
Move users between OUs as roles change
Disable (don't delete) when someone leaves — preserves history and access references

p: OUs group objects for management and Group Policy. Placing a user in the right OU determines which policies and access they inherit.

note.text: Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC) is the everyday GUI; PowerShell (Get-ADUser, New-ADUser) scales the same tasks.

content.practice: Outline the steps to onboard a new hire's account and place them in the correct OU for their department.

quiz.p: When a user leaves, the safer first action is to…
quiz.ex: Disabling preserves history/access references; deletion can be done later.

quiz.p: A user's OU placement determines…
o: Which Group Policy and access they inherit
quiz.ex: OU membership drives inherited policy and access.

quiz.p: The everyday GUI for AD account tasks is…
quiz.ex: ADUC manages users, groups, and OUs.

content.intro: Access problems usually come down to group membership. Fixing them means understanding how groups grant rights.

p: Permissions are assigned to groups; users get access by being members. To grant or remove access, change group membership — not per-user permissions.

ul: Confirm the user is in the right group
Remember group changes apply at next logon (or token refresh)
Check for a Deny that overrides Allow

note.text: If access still fails after correct membership, the resource's permissions or a GPO may be involved — gather details and escalate.

content.practice: A user can't open a shared folder their teammates can. List the first three things you'd check.

quiz.p: To grant a user access to a resource you usually…
o: Add them to the right group
quiz.ex: Access is granted via group membership.

quiz.p: New group membership typically takes effect…
quiz.ex: Users often must log off/on to pick up new membership.

quiz.p: If one group Allows and another Denies, the result is…
quiz.ex: An explicit Deny overrides Allow.

content.intro: Password resets and account lockouts are the bread and butter of support — do them correctly and securely.

ul.t: the account is locked from failed attempts — unlock it.
set a new password (require change at next logon).

p: Always confirm you're talking to the real user (per your verification policy) before resetting — password resets are a classic social-engineering target.

note.text: Recurring lockouts often come from a stale password cached on a phone, mapped drive, or service — find the source, don't just keep unlocking.

content.practice: A user is locked out for the third time today. Explain what you'd investigate beyond simply unlocking them.

quiz.p: Before resetting a password you must first…
quiz.ex: Identity verification prevents social-engineering resets.

quiz.p: An account locked by failed attempts needs to be…
quiz.ex: Unlock the account (reset only if the password is unknown).

quiz.p: Repeated lockouts are commonly caused by…
quiz.ex: Cached old credentials repeatedly lock the account.

content.intro: You don't have to author policy, but Tier 2 must recognise when Group Policy is the cause and do first-line checks.

p: Group Policy centrally enforces settings (drive maps, security, restrictions) on users and computers based on their OU. A 'weird setting I can't change' is often a GPO.

ul.t: — reapply policy.
— see which GPOs applied to the user/PC.

note.text: If a policy is misapplied or missing, capture the gpresult output and escalate to the team that manages GPOs — don't edit domain policy from the help desk.

content.practice: A user says a mapped drive vanished. Show the two commands you'd run to check whether Group Policy is responsible.

quiz.p: A setting a user 'can't change' is often enforced by…
quiz.ex: GPOs enforce settings centrally based on OU.

quiz.p: Which command reports the GPOs applied to a user/PC?
quiz.ex: gpresult shows the resultant set of policy.

quiz.p: From the help desk, a misapplied domain GPO should be…
o: Documented and escalated to the GPO team
quiz.ex: Capture evidence and escalate; don't edit domain policy at Tier 2.

courses.title: Tier 2: Microsoft 365 Administration
courses.description: Support the cloud productivity stack every business runs on — the admin center, licensing, Exchange Online, identity and MFA, and Teams/SharePoint/Intune basics.

content.intro: The Microsoft 365 admin center is where you manage users, licenses, and services. Tier 2 lives here daily.

ul: Users: create, reset passwords, assign licenses, block sign-in
Groups: Microsoft 365 groups, distribution lists, security groups
Services: Exchange, SharePoint, Teams settings and health

p: Least privilege applies: assign specific roles (e.g. Helpdesk Admin, User Admin) rather than Global Admin. Global Admin is powerful and should be rare.

note.text: Before deep-diving a 'everything's down' ticket, check the Service health dashboard — the issue may be a Microsoft-side incident.

content.practice: In the admin center (or from memory), list where you'd go to reset a password, assign a license, and check if Outlook is down for everyone.

quiz.p: Which admin role follows least privilege for help desk work?
quiz.ex: Scoped roles like Helpdesk Admin avoid over-granting Global Admin.

quiz.p: Before troubleshooting a widespread outage, check…
quiz.ex: Service health shows Microsoft-side incidents.

quiz.p: The admin center is primarily used to manage…
quiz.ex: It manages M365 identities, licensing, and services.

content.intro: Licensing decides which apps and features a user gets. Assigning the right plan — and spotting the wrong one — is a common Tier 2 task.

ul.t: web/mobile apps + Exchange, Teams, SharePoint (no desktop Office).
adds the desktop Office (Microsoft 365) apps.
Standard + advanced security and device management (Intune).
the Office apps only, without the services.
enterprise apps + services and core security/compliance.
E3 plus advanced security, analytics, and voice.

note.text: 'Outlook won't activate' or 'no desktop apps' is often a Basic/Apps license where the user needs Standard/E3 — check and reassign.

content.practice: A user on Business Basic says the Outlook desktop app won't activate. Explain the likely cause and fix.

quiz.p: Which plan does NOT include the desktop Office apps?
quiz.ex: Business Basic is web/mobile + services; no desktop Office.

quiz.p: Business Premium adds, over Standard, mainly…
quiz.ex: Premium adds security and Intune device management.

quiz.p: A user with no desktop apps who needs them likely has the wrong…
quiz.ex: Reassign to a plan that includes desktop Office (Standard/E3).

content.intro: Email is the highest-volume M365 support area. These are the mailbox concepts Tier 2 handles.

ul.t: a person's mailbox.
a no-license mailbox several users access (e.g. support@).
delivers to a group of recipients.

ul: Grant access/Send As to a shared mailbox
Add an alias (extra address) to a mailbox
Release a message from quarantine

note.text: For 'I didn't get an email', check quarantine, the recipient address, and message trace before assuming a server problem.

content.practice: A team needs everyone to send from support@company.com. Describe the mailbox type and access you'd set up.

quiz.p: A support@ address several staff monitor is best set up as a…
quiz.ex: A shared mailbox lets multiple users access one inbox.

quiz.p: An extra email address on an existing mailbox is called an…
quiz.ex: An alias is an additional address for a mailbox.

quiz.p: For a missing inbound email, first check…
quiz.ex: Quarantine and message trace explain most delivery issues.

content.intro: Microsoft 365 identity runs on Entra ID. Multi-factor authentication and conditional access are core to securing it — and to the tickets you'll see.

p: The cloud identity behind M365 — accounts, sign-in, and access policies live here. It may sync from on-prem AD (hybrid identity).

ul.t: a second factor (app/code) beyond the password — the biggest single security win.
lets users reset their own password after verifying.

note.text: Conditional Access allows/blocks sign-ins based on conditions (location, device, risk). A blocked login may be policy working as intended — check before 'fixing' it.

content.practice: A user is prompted for MFA from a new country and blocked. Explain what could be happening before you change anything.

quiz.p: Microsoft 365 cloud identity is provided by…
quiz.ex: Entra ID underpins M365 identity and sign-in.

quiz.p: The single biggest account-security improvement is…
quiz.ex: MFA dramatically reduces account compromise.

quiz.p: A sign-in blocked by location policy is likely…
quiz.ex: Conditional Access may be correctly blocking risky sign-ins.

content.intro: Beyond email, Tier 2 supports collaboration and managed devices. Here's the lay of the land.

ul.t: chat/meetings; issues are often audio/video devices or membership.
file storage and sharing; issues are often permissions or sync.

p: Most 'I can't open this file' tickets are sharing/permission problems — confirm who owns it and how it was shared.

note.text: Intune manages and secures devices — enrollment, compliance policies, and app deployment. Enrollment/compliance is a growing Tier 2 area.

content.practice: A user can't edit a shared SharePoint document. List the first two things you'd verify.

quiz.p: Most 'can't open a shared file' tickets are…
quiz.ex: Permissions/sharing cause most file-access issues.

quiz.p: Intune is used to…
quiz.ex: Intune handles device enrollment, compliance, and apps.

quiz.p: A Teams meeting with no sound is usually a…
quiz.ex: Teams AV issues are typically device/permission related.

courses.title: Tier 2: Network Troubleshooting
courses.description: Resolve the connectivity tickets that get escalated past Tier 1 — client addressing and DNS, VPN and remote access, and networked printers.

content.intro: Most 'no internet' tickets come down to addressing or DNS on the client. A quick sequence isolates it.

ul.t: no DHCP lease — check adapter, cable, or DHCP.
test the gateway, then a public IP, then a name.

sections.code:
ipconfig /all        # see IP, gateway, DNS
ipconfig /flushdns   # clear a stale DNS cache
nslookup example.com # confirm resolution

note.text: ipconfig /release then /renew re-requests a lease; flushing DNS fixes stale-record issues.

content.practice: Walk through the exact commands you'd run for 'I can ping 8.8.8.8 but websites won't load'.

quiz.p: A client with a 169.254 address has…
quiz.ex: 169.254 (APIPA) means no DHCP lease was obtained.

quiz.p: Pinging an IP works but names fail — fix by checking/refreshing…
quiz.ex: IP works, names fail → DNS resolution problem.

quiz.p: Which re-requests a DHCP lease?
quiz.ex: release/renew re-acquires an address from DHCP.

content.intro: Remote workers depend on VPN. When it fails, a few checks cover most cases.

ul: Verify credentials/MFA and that the account isn't locked
Confirm internet works before the VPN connects
Check the client is current and the profile/config is correct

p: Often DNS or routing: is the VPN pushing the right DNS and routes? Split tunneling sends only some traffic through the VPN.

note.text: Gateway-side outages or certificate/policy problems are beyond the client — gather the error and escalate with details.

content.practice: A user connects to VPN but can't reach the file server. Name two likely causes and how you'd check them.

quiz.p: Before a VPN can connect, the user needs…
quiz.ex: VPN rides over the existing internet connection.

quiz.p: Connected to VPN but can't reach internal resources often means…
o: DNS/routing not applied through the tunnel
quiz.ex: Missing VPN DNS/routes block internal access.

quiz.p: Split tunneling means…
o: Only some traffic goes through the VPN
quiz.ex: Split tunneling routes only selected traffic through the VPN.

content.intro: Networked printers generate steady tickets. Knowing the moving parts makes them quick.

ul: The printer has an IP; the PC prints via a queue/driver to that IP or a print server
A print server centralises queues and drivers for many users

ul.t: clear jobs / restart the Print Spooler service.
reinstall the correct model driver.
check power, network/IP, and connectivity (ping it).

note.text: Restarting the Print Spooler clears all queued jobs on that machine — warn users first.

content.practice: A shared printer shows 'offline' for everyone. List the checks you'd run from the print server outward.

quiz.p: A stuck print queue is often cleared by…
o: Clearing jobs / restarting the Print Spooler
quiz.ex: The Print Spooler service manages the queue.

quiz.p: A networked printer 'offline' for everyone suggests checking…
quiz.ex: A shared outage points to the printer/network, not one PC.

quiz.p: Restarting the Print Spooler on a print server…
o: Clears all queued jobs there — warn users
quiz.ex: It flushes queued jobs, so notify affected users.

courses.title: Tier 2: ITIL & Escalation
courses.description: Work like a professional service desk — incident vs problem vs change, priorities and SLAs, escalation paths, and documentation that makes you trusted.

content.intro: ITIL gives support a shared vocabulary. Three terms cover most of what you'll do — and confusing them causes chaos.

ul.t: restore service now (the printer is down — fix it).
find and remove the root cause of repeated incidents.
a controlled modification to prevent or fix issues (with approval).

p: Incidents restore service fast; problems stop them recurring; changes are made safely with review. Treating a risky change like a quick fix is how outages happen.

note.text: Log every incident, link repeats to a problem record, and route infrastructure modifications through change control.

content.practice: Classify each as incident, problem, or change: 'email is down now', 'email drops every Monday', 'upgrade the mail connector next week'.

quiz.p: Restoring a down service as fast as possible is a(n)…
quiz.ex: An incident is about restoring service quickly.

quiz.p: Finding the root cause of recurring incidents is…
quiz.ex: Problem management removes the underlying cause.

quiz.p: A controlled, approved modification to infrastructure is a…
quiz.ex: Changes go through review/approval to reduce risk.

content.intro: Not every ticket is equal. Priority and SLAs decide order, and escalation gets the right help without dropping ownership.

p: Priority = impact (how many/how critical) × urgency (how time-sensitive). A single-user cosmetic issue is low; a site-wide outage is top priority.
A Service Level Agreement sets target response/resolution times per priority. Meeting SLAs is how the desk is measured.

sections.caption: Escalate up a tier only when needed — and keep ownership until it's resolved.

note.text: Escalating doesn't mean walking away — hand off with full notes and follow the ticket to closure.

content.practice: Assign a priority to: one user's font looks wrong vs the whole office can't log in. Justify each.

quiz.p: Priority is generally determined by…
quiz.ex: Priority = impact × urgency.

quiz.p: An SLA defines…
quiz.ex: SLAs set time targets per priority.

quiz.p: When you escalate a ticket you should…
o: Hand off with full notes and keep ownership
quiz.ex: Escalation includes documentation and continued ownership.

content.intro: Good notes and knowledge articles multiply your value — they speed resolution, enable handoffs, and prevent repeat work.

p: Record the symptom, what you checked, what you changed, and the outcome — enough that a colleague could pick it up cold.

ul: Write a KB article for issues that recur
Keep steps clear and current
Link tickets to the article you used

note.text: When remoting onto a user's machine, explain what you're doing, get consent, and respect their privacy — trust is part of support.

content.practice: Write two-sentence ticket notes for a password reset you completed, good enough for a colleague to understand cold.

quiz.p: Good ticket notes let a colleague…
quiz.ex: Clear notes enable seamless handoffs.

quiz.p: A recurring issue with known steps deserves a…
quiz.ex: KB articles capture repeatable resolutions.

quiz.p: When remoting onto a user's PC you should…
quiz.ex: Consent and transparency build user trust.
